# Draft:Battle of the Three Roads

----
Battle of the Three Roads - During the Battle of the Three Roads, the Mongolian government sent troops to the Three Roads to protect the Khovd region and liberate Western Mongolia or Xinjiang from China. There is almost no research on this and there is only a small amount of information in the sources. The Mongol-Chinese war that took place separately from the Battle of the Five Roads was called the Battle of the Three Roads.
When the Bogd Khan declared the establishment of the Mongol Empire, the six assemblies of Inner Mongolia, including Zuu Ud, Zost, Zhirem, Shiliin Gol, Ulaancav, and Ikh Zuu, expressed their gratitude and joy, and sent troops from the capital circle to liberate the entire Inner Mongolia. 35 of the 49 districts of the Barga and Inner Six Districts of Hulunbuyir joined Mongolia, in addition to 24 districts of Khokhnuur, 8 districts of Tsakhar, and 16 districts of Ilin Gol and Tarvagatai. By decree of Bogd Khan, a special department was established in July 1913 to administer the affairs of the eastern region, and the wise and noble Galsandashi, a member of the Tsetsen Khan aimag, was appointed as its Minister.
Prerequisites
After the establishment of the Bogd Khanate of Mongolia, the Mongolian authorities at that time sought to unite the Mongolian nation and establish a Unified Mongolian State. The Bogd Khanate expressed its desire for Inner Mongolia and other Mongols to unite in Mongolia, and uprisings and movements were taking place everywhere among the Mongols under the former Manchu Qing Dynasty. In response, the Chinese, who had overthrown the Manchu Qing Dynasty and established the Middle Kingdom, considered themselves the heirs of the Manchus and crushed the resistance and struggle of the nations that had emerged in the former Manchu Qing Dynasty with the desire for independence by military and armed force. At such a critical time in history, the Bogd Khan moved a large army in three directions to liberate Mongolia and the Western Mongols from Chinese oppression, unite the Mongols who had voluntarily joined him, and defend their borders. In November 1912, a meeting of all the Chinese people was held to discuss the invasion of Mongolia, and the attitude of the Beijing authorities became clear. At the same time, the situation in the borderlands became tense. The Altai Minister of Affairs, following Beijing's instructions, had mobilized 10,000 troops and made the situation in the western border even more difficult. Therefore, the Mongolian side sent Magsarjav back to the Khovd region with Ulias, and mobilized 4,000 troops from many provinces, including Khalkh, Dorvet, and Tagna Uriankhai, to be installed under their command. In this way, Balt's plan was thwarted, but soon in the summer of 1913, the Kazakhs, who had joined the army, changed their minds and crossed the Chinese territory of Altai, while some of them fled to places such as Khushoomod, Russia, and returned, plundering the Mongols of Dorvet and Uriankhai. For this reason, Magsarjav took a thousand soldiers and went to the Altai Mountains, the foothills, the Sagsai River, and Lake Tolbo to expel the traitors from Mongolian territory. In the early winter of 1913, he quelled the unrest near the Hushoo Tree, stayed there for two more months, and participated in negotiations on the issue of the fugitive Kazakhs, before returning to the Khovd River. Based on these foreign political situations, the Bogd Khan government sent troops to the western and southern borders, such as Khovd, Dariganga, and the Eguzer monasteries in 1912, and to the Dariganga, Soned, Ulaancav directions and other places in the foothills in early 1913. Yuan Shikai's government did not recognize Mongolian independence and directed a large army towards Mongolia in order to suppress it by force. At the end of 1912, troops were deployed in cities near the border such as Batkhaalga, Dolon Nuur, and Khaalga (Re He), and on October 12, 1912, military detachments were deployed in the direction of Shar Sum, Khokh Hot, and Khaalgan.
Combat operations
Having received news that the Mongolian army had liberated Khovd and had deployed troops to protect the border in Gurvan Tsang, a Chinese military detachment set off from a place called Tsagduult (15 miles from Beijing) in 1912 and came to Tsagaan Nulkhed for the winter, planning to defeat the Mongolian army in the summer of 1913. At this time, the khutagt served as the minister in charge of the western border, and the deputy taij Bayar (who became a duke of the state by the Bogd decree of November 12, 1913) served as the assistant to the governor. On June 1, 1913, a battle took place between the Mongolian and Chinese troops at the Ulaan Khair Khan in the White Plains, resulting in 22 Mongolian casualties and 30 wounded. On the 7th of the same month, two battles took place there, involving more than 700 Mongolian and about 2,000 Chinese troops, with about 20 Chinese soldiers killed and 50 horses captured. On July 17, a battle was fought with more than 300 Chinese troops. In July 1913, the Mongolian army divided into three routes and attacked westward. One route left Uriankhai and crossed the Bulgan River. The other two routes were attacked by the troops of Bao Qingdong and Wu Yunzhi, respectively, and the Chinese Khovd auxiliary troops were severely beaten, resulting in a heavy defeat for more than 300 soldiers and more than 500 casualties. At the request of the Mongols, the Russian government, in order to strengthen its position in Mongolia, sent a Kazakh military detachment from the city of Ulaan Ud (Ulaan Ud) to Khovd through Ikh Khurey, and in the summer sent a 3,000-strong infantry and artillery detachment from Biysk to Khovd. The arrival of the Russian military detachment in Khovd in the summer of 1913 weakened the Chinese military activity and forced them to withdraw their troops from the White Plains. The opposition of Russian diplomats and the placement of some Russian military units in the sensitive Khovd region and Niyslel Khurey stopped the Chinese army from conquering Mongolia.
